title: Six answers that dodge
hookLine: the king recounts six well-known teachers; none answered his question

lines: A SIMPLE QUESTION AT THE HELP DESK.
cards: You ask a simple question at the help desk: will my package arrive by Friday? And you get a long, confident answer about the history of shipping. Polite, maybe even brilliant.
But it isn't an answer. King Ajatasattu has had that experience six times. When he asks the Buddha what the contemplative life is good for, the Buddha asks him back: have you asked anyone else?
Yes, says the king. Six well-known teachers. And he tells what each one said.

teach.h: THE KING'S ACCOUNT OF SIX TEACHERS
teach.b: Here's the king's account. Purana Kassapa told him deeds bring no merit and no evil, whatever one does.
Makkhali Gosala told him beings are purified only by wandering through countless lives, as fixed as a ball of string that unrolls to its end.
Ajita of the hair blanket said nothing survives the body, which breaks into earth, water, fire and air.
Pakudha Kaccayana said there are seven unchanging substances, so even a sword through a head only passes between them. Nigantha Nataputta told him about a fourfold restraint.
And Sanjaya Belatthiputta wouldn't commit to anything: I don't say it's so, I don't say it's not so, I don't say it's neither. The texts call that eel-wriggling. Two things matter here.

teach.h: A BUDDHIST TEXT'S SUMMARY, NOT THEIRS
teach.b: First, this is the king's summary, inside a Buddhist text. These teachers had their own followers, who would describe them in their own terms.
Nigantha Nataputta is traditionally identified with Mahavira, whom Jains revere, and Jains have their own scriptures and understanding of his teaching.

The discourse isn't a fair hearing of six philosophies, and doesn't claim to be. Second, the king's point: whatever their merits, none of them answered his question. He asked about a fruit visible here and now.
It was like asking about a mango and being told about a breadfruit.
And he didn't scold any of them; a king, he thought, shouldn't insult a renunciant in his own realm.
He just got up and left, still carrying his question.

how: Buddhist teachers often use this passage to illustrate how the Buddha's contemporaries were remembered in Buddhist sources; Jain tradition preserves its own scriptures and account of Mahavira's teaching.

o: a monk's restless fidgeting while sitting
dodging a question, committing to nothing
a sly lie told to win an argument

games.q: six answers that dodge: tap the pairs.
p: identified with Mahavira of the Jains

s: the discourse gives a full and fair hearing of six philosophies
it's the king's short summary inside a Buddhist text; their own followers would describe them differently.
the king's complaint is that none answered his actual question
he asked about a visible fruit, and got answers about something else.
the king insulted each teacher before leaving
he thought a king shouldn't insult a renunciant in his realm, and simply left.

games.q: you're the king. you asked a well-known teacher what fruit practice gives here and now, and got a long answer about something else. what do you do?
o: say nothing against him, get up and leave.
have him banished from the kingdom.
games.why: the king neither approved nor rejected the answer. he didn't insult a renunciant in his own realm. he got up and left, still carrying his question.

practice: Think of a question you've asked lately that never got a straight answer, from a person, an institution, or yourself, and say the real question plainly inside: what I actually want to know is this.
Then notice whether someone asked you something you answered with something else, and just see it.

wordCard.voice: Eel-wriggling. What the texts call Sanjaya's refusal to commit to any answer: the king asked about a fruit visible here and now, and six times was told about something else.

orig.note: Pali amaravikkhepa: eel-wriggling, slipping out of every question without committing.

carryVoice: Your line: they didn't answer. He asked about a mango and was told about a breadfruit. Go gently.
